_comment: Crop facts used by the rotation explorer. Values are written for Central Texas (Blackland Prairie and Post Oak Savannah, USDA zone 8b, about 750-900 mm of rain a year) and are simplified to low/medium/high so rules can use them. They are a starting point: check them with your county extension agent before relying on them. Each crop lists the sources the values were read from. Months are 1=January .. 12=December. 'growing_months' are months of active growth; 'in_ground_months' also include months a perennial is dormant but still covers and roots the soil.

crops.name: Bermudagrass
crops.soil_note: A perennial sod keeps living roots and cover on the soil all year, which holds soil in place and lets rain soak in.
risks: Needs nitrogen fertilizer to stay productive; costs rise with fertilizer prices.
Fall armyworms can strip pastures in late summer; scout after rains.

sources.title: Forage Bermudagrass: Selection, Establishment and Management (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

crops.name: Native warm-season grass mix
crops.soil_note: Native grasses such as switchgrass root more than 3 m (10 ft) deep, adding organic matter deep in the soil and opening channels for water.
risks: Slow to establish: expect one to three years before a full stand, with weed control in the first year.
Seed of local ecotypes can be costly; ask your NRCS office about cost-share programs.

sources.title: Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) Plant Guide (USDA NRCS)
'Alamo' switchgrass Conservation Plant Release (USDA NRCS Texas)

crops.name: Sorghum-sudangrass
crops.soil_note: Few crops add as much organic matter; mowing it once pushes roots deeper so they break up compacted subsoil.
risks: Can cause prussic acid poisoning in livestock when young, drought-stressed or frosted; follow grazing guidelines.
Needs good fertility, usually extra nitrogen, to produce well.

sources.title: Sorghum Sudangrass, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed. (SARE)

crops.name: Forage oats
crops.soil_note: Quick fall cover that protects bare soil over winter and feeds livestock when warm-season grass is dormant.
risks: Less cold hardy than wheat or ryegrass; a hard freeze can thin the stand.
Leaf rust is common in wet springs; choose resistant varieties.

sources.title: Oats, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed. (SARE)

crops.name: Annual ryegrass
crops.soil_note: Its dense, fibrous roots hold soil and improve structure, and it grows on clay and poorly drained soils where small grains struggle.
risks: Can become a serious weed in following wheat or oat crops in the Southern Plains, and has developed herbicide resistance.
A heavy user of soil moisture; performs poorly in drought.

sources.title: Annual Ryegrass, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed. (SARE)

crops.name: Crimson clover
crops.soil_note: A legume: bacteria in its root nodules take nitrogen from the air, so the next crop needs less fertilizer.
risks: Fares poorly on heavy clay and waterlogged soils.
Dry soil in fall often hinders establishment in the South.

sources.title: Crimson Clover, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed. (SARE)

crops.name: Hairy vetch
crops.soil_note: One of the top nitrogen-fixing covers (often replacing most nitrogen fertilizer for the next crop) and it loosens topsoil, though its residue breaks down fast and builds little long-term organic matter.
risks: Hard seed can make it a weed in later crops if it is allowed to set seed; time termination carefully.
Viny growth can tangle equipment; mixing with a cereal helps.

sources.title: Hairy Vetch, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed. (SARE)

crops.name: Cowpea
crops.soil_note: A drought-tolerant summer legume: it fixes nitrogen and its taproots can reach about 2.4 m (8 ft) for water.
risks: Less tolerant of waterlogging than soybeans; seed rots in cool, wet soils.
Weedy if rain falls just after planting, before the canopy closes.

sources.title: Cowpeas, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed. (SARE)

crops.name: Sunn hemp
crops.soil_note: A fast summer legume: in 8 to 12 weeks it can produce over 2,200 kg/ha (5,000 lb/acre) of biomass and fix over 110 kg/ha (100 lb/acre) of nitrogen.
risks: Seed supply is limited and can be expensive.
Tall, fibrous stems can be hard to terminate if left too long.

sources.title: Sunn Hemp: A Cover Crop for Southern Farming Systems (USDA NRCS)
Sunn Hemp (Crotalaria juncea) Plant Guide (USDA NRCS)

crops.name: Winter wheat (cover crop)
crops.soil_note: A cereal cover that holds soil over winter, takes up leftover nitrogen so it does not wash away, and leaves long-lasting residue.
risks: Can host the same diseases and insects as a wheat or oat grain crop that follows it.
Must be terminated early enough that it does not dry out the soil for the next crop.

sources.title: Winter Wheat, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed. (SARE)

crops.name: Corn
crops.soil_note: Leaves a lot of residue that can protect the soil if it is left on the surface.
risks: Heat and drought during pollination (late May to June) cut yields and raise the risk of aflatoxin.
Needs more water than sorghum to produce its first bushel of grain.

sources.title: Corn in Texas, crop brief (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)
Managing Insect and Mite Pests of Texas Corn (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

crops.name: Grain sorghum
crops.soil_note: A drought-tolerant grain that needs less water than corn and leaves heavy residue to protect the soil.
risks: Sugarcane aphids and headworms need scouting through the season.
Rotating with other crops helps break insect, weed and disease cycles.

sources.title: Sorghum in Texas, crop brief (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)
Agronomic Management for Texas Panhandle Sorghum, SCSC-2026-09 (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

crops.name: Cotton
crops.soil_note: Its deep taproot reaches water lower in the profile, but it leaves little residue, so a cover crop after harvest protects the soil.
risks: Cotton root rot is common on the alkaline clay soils of Central Texas.
Fleahoppers and other insects need scouting; wet fields can delay planting and harvest.

sources.title: Cotton in Texas, crop brief (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)
Managing Cotton Insects in Texas (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

crops.name: Soybean
crops.soil_note: A legume grain crop that fixes much of its own nitrogen, though its light residue leaves soil exposed after harvest.
risks: Stink bugs and other insects need scouting in late summer.
Late-season drought on dryland fields cuts yields; planting on beds helps drainage in wet areas.

sources.title: Managing Soybean Insects in Texas (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

crops.name: Winter wheat (grain)
crops.soil_note: Covers the soil through the wet winter and spring and can be grazed in winter as a dual-purpose crop.
risks: Grazing past first hollow stem lowers grain yield; follow grazing-termination guidelines.
Rust and other leaf diseases are worse in wet springs.

sources.title: Texas Small Grains Production Practices (Texas A&M AgriLife)
Winter Wheat Management Calendar (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)
